To renege means to go back on a promise, agreement, or commitment you have already made. When someone reneges, they agreed to do something — and then chose not to do it, even though the other person was counting on them.

Think of it simply: You make a deal with someone. You both agree on the terms. Then later, one person simply doesn't follow through. They reneged.

This is important grammar to know. You almost never use "renege" alone — you renege on something. This is its standard pattern:

  • renege on a promise
  • renege on a deal
  • renege on an agreement
  • renege on a commitment
  • renege on a contract

So you would say "She reneged on her promise," not "She reneged her promise." The preposition "on" is essentially glued to this word.

This is the most important thing to understand. Renege is not a neutral word. It carries a strong negative judgment. When you say someone reneged, you are not simply saying they failed to do what they said — you are implying that they chose not to, and that this was a moral failure on their part. The word quietly signals betrayal of trust, bad faith, and unreliability.

This is why "renege" feels heavier and more accusatory than just saying "they didn't keep their promise." The word has weight and sting to it. If someone reneged, they knew exactly what they committed to, and they still didn't honor it — and the person on the other side was left in the lurch because of it.

Seeing the word in different situations is the best way to lock in its meaning.

In business: A company agrees to pay its supplier by the end of the month. When the deadline arrives, the company refuses to pay and walks away from the deal. The supplier rightfully says: "They reneged on our agreement."

In politics: A politician campaigns loudly on a promise to cut taxes. Once elected, they raise taxes instead. Citizens feel deceived and say: "The government reneged on its campaign promise."

In a personal situation: Your friend promises to help you move apartments on Saturday. On Friday night, without a real reason, he texts to say he's not coming. You tell others: "He reneged on his promise to help me."

In a negotiation: Two people negotiate the sale of a house. They agree on a price and shake hands. But right before signing, the buyer suddenly demands a much lower price. The seller says: "The buyer reneged on the deal we had made."

In every case, notice the same pattern: a commitment was made, trust was extended, and then that trust was broken.

The subject of "renege" is always an entity capable of making conscious decisions — a person, a company, a government, an organization. You would not say the weather reneged, or that a machine reneged. It applies only to those who can make and break deliberate commitments.

Understanding the words around it will sharpen your sense of exactly what "renege" means and when to use it.

"Break a promise" is the everyday, casual equivalent. It means the same thing but is softer and more common in speech. "Renege" is more formal and feels more accusatory.

"Back out" means to withdraw from something, but it is largely neutral. Someone might back out of a deal because of a genuine emergency and you wouldn't judge them harshly for it. But when you say someone reneged, you are making a moral accusation — that they acted in bad faith.

"Go back on one's word" is very close in meaning to renege and is slightly less formal. Both carry the sense of a moral failure.

"Withdraw" is the most neutral of all. To withdraw from an agreement just means to remove yourself from it. No blame is implied whatsoever.

What sets "renege" apart from all of these is the element of betrayal. The word doesn't just describe the action — it judges it.

Renege is a formal to semi-formal word. You're more likely to encounter it in journalism ("The government reneged on the peace deal"), business ("The contractor reneged on the terms"), or serious conversations about trust and accountability. In casual everyday speech, people more often say "he went back on his word" or "she broke her promise." But when you want to sound more serious, precise, or formal — and when you want to convey a clear sense of bad faith — "renege" is the right word.

To renege on something means to break a commitment you have already made — to say you'll do something and then choose not to. The word is accusatory by nature: it implies bad faith, unreliability, and a betrayal of trust. It almost always takes the preposition "on." It is a formal word, used in serious contexts, and it carries a clear moral judgment against whoever does it. If you've been wronged by someone who didn't honor their word — especially in a serious or formal context — "renege" is precisely the word you're looking for.
